science.title: Genomic analysis links phage susceptibility to the K5 capsule in uropathogenic Escherichia coli
science.description: Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) is the leading cause of urinary tract infections, which can progress to bloodstream infections, while the increasing prevalence of extended-spectrum β-lactamase (ESBL)-producing strains limits treatment options. Although bacteriophage (phage) therapy is promising, identifying effective phages is resource-intensive. Genomic predictors of phage susceptibility could facilitate phage selection; however, the underlying bacterial traits remain uncharacterized. Here, 49 ESBL-producing UPEC clinical isolates and 42 phages were analysed to investigate bacterial genomic features associated with the phage susceptibility. Independent susceptibility clustering and genome-wide association analyses facilitated identification of K5 capsule biosynthesis genes as shared genomic features associated with susceptibility to specific phage clusters. The K5 strains were broadly susceptible, whereas three strains remained nonsusceptible; genome analysis revealed mutations in capsule biosynthesis genes linked to reduced capsular polysaccharide levels. Phage adsorption assays using the K5 capsule fraction supported the K5 capsule as a receptor for these phage clusters. Furthermore, phages associated with K5 susceptibility were predicted to encode putative depolymerases similar to K5 lyase, extending this mechanism to phages effective against ESBL-producing UPEC. These results support the K5 capsule as a receptor for phages targeting ESBL-producing UPEC and highlight its potential as a predictor of phage susceptibility.

science.title: Relationships between reproductive steroids, glandular microbiota, and volatile chemical signals in naturally cycling versus hormonally contracepted female lemurs
science.description: Olfactory communication directs socio-reproductive interaction in animals, but underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Endocrine action and microbial fermentation both influence the manufacture, composition, and expression of vertebrate chemosignals, involving volatile organic compounds (VOCs); however, there has been no integrative investigation of a putative tripart relationship between reproductive hormones, microbes, and VOCs. Our longitudinal experimental study of normative and contracepted females characterizes pairwise and tripart relationships in two scent-marking primates: ring-tailed lemurs (Lemur catta) and Coquerel’s sifakas (Propithicus coquereli). We used (1) serum enzyme immunoassays to quantify progesterone (P4), estradiol (E2), and the synthetic progestogen, medroxyprogesterone acetate (MPA), (2) Illumina sequencing of the bacterial 16 S rRNA gene to identify microbiota in genital (labial) secretions, and (3) gas chromatography-mass spectrometry to characterize labial VOCs. Despite species differences in hormone concentrations, contraception expectedly muted natural variation in the E2/P4 ratio and introduced initially supraphysiological MPA concentrations. Normative and induced hormonal variation was reflected in the microbial and/or chemical composition of labial secretions; however, predictive power varied by species, potentially reflecting socioecological variation or differences in glandular specialization. These results highlight the importance of cyclical endocrine variation in female reproductive signaling and the overriding effects on VOC manufacture of a disturbed glandular microbiome during contraception.

science.title: Spatial distribution patterns and quantitative analysis of traditional villages in the Qiantang River Basin using geographic detectors
science.description: The distribution pattern and agglomeration characteristics of traditional villages play a crucial role as historical and cultural assets in rural development, emphasizing the significance of regional cultural preservation and rural revitalization. This study examines 362 national traditional villages in the Qiantang River Basin (QRB) in Zhejiang to uncover their spatial settlement patterns and analyze the influencing factors. Employing spatial analysis methods such as the nearest neighbor index, geographical concentration index, and kernel density estimation, the study elucidates the spatial distribution of these villages. Utilizing the geographical detector model, it identifies key factors associated with their spatial distribution, quantitatively assessing their explanatory power and interaction patterns among natural, economic, and cultural dimensions. The study also suggests strategies for the protection and sustainable use of traditional villages in the QRB. The research findings reveal that traditional villages in the QRB exhibit a clustered distribution pattern, characterized by a spatial structure of “two cores and multiple clusters”. This agglomeration tendency is observed at the county level, with a distinct pattern of concentration in the southwestern mountainous regions and sparsity in the northeastern plains. Various factors such as slope, altitude, per capita disposable income, road network density, and the proportion of the primary industry play significant roles in shaping the spatial distribution of these traditional villages. A multifactor detection model demonstrates that the distribution pattern of traditional villages in the QRB is a result of the dynamic interplay between natural features and human influences. The impact of each factor varies across different stages, highlighting the complex nature of village distribution. This quantitative analysis assesses the varying degrees of influence exerted by the natural environment, socioeconomic conditions, and historical heritage on the distribution of traditional villages, addressing limitations of previous qualitative studies. This study not only enhances our understanding of the factors driving the distribution of traditional villages but also provides a scientific foundation for the strategic conservation of these villages in the QRB and the management of cultural heritage on a basin-wide scale.
